title: CS102_Unit2a_Unit_2
summary: Positions Unit 2 within the overall course roadmap: after Unit 1's scalar (IPO) processing, Unit 2 covers linear (1D) processing, followed by multidimensional processing (Unit 3) and divide & conquer/functional decomposition (Unit 4).
main_text:
Unit 1: Scalar processing (aka IPO = Input-Process-Output Programs).
Unit 2: Linear (1D) Processing.
Unit 3: Multidimensional Processing.
Unit 4: Divide & Conquer (Functional Decomposition).
notes_text: This roadmap slide grays out Units 1, 3, and 4 to emphasize that Unit 2 (Linear/1D Processing) is the current focus.

images.description: Four stacked icon diagrams representing increasing data complexity across the course units: a single input/output pair through a CPU chip (Unit 1, scalar), a short array of inputs/outputs through a chip (Unit 2, linear/1D), a grid of arrays through a chip (Unit 3, multidimensional), and a set of function blocks f(x) and g(y) (Unit 4, functional decomposition).

title: CS102_Unit2a_Linear_1D_Processing_Programs
summary: Defines linear (1D) processing programs as those that process arbitrary-length sequences of data using a loop, following a Prompt-Input-Process-Output cycle, illustrated with two worked terminal examples (averaging scores and counting gym workout streaks).
main_text:
Process an arbitrary length (or large fixed-length) sequence or set of data. The distinguishing feature is the use of a LOOP to perform the same/similar processing repetitively on each data item. We will likely still keep our general structure but with some sequence of those operations repeated via the loop: Prompt, Input, Process, Output.

Example 1: 'Enter student scores (end with -1)' with inputs 80, 90, 72, -1 produces 'The average score is 80.6667'.
Example 2: 'For each day of the week, indicate if you worked out at the gym: yes no yes yes yes no yes' produces 'You worked out 5 days with a max streak of 3 days in a row.'
notes_text: Numbered annotations (1-4) on both terminal examples map to the Prompt/Input/Process/Output stages, showing how the same 4-stage structure recurs across different loop-based programs.

images.description: An icon diagram showing a small array of inputs feeding into a CPU chip and producing a small array of outputs, symbolizing linear (1D) processing of a sequence of data.

Two annotated terminal-style transcripts demonstrating linear processing programs: one prompts for and averages a sequence of student scores ending in a sentinel value of -1, the other reads a week of yes/no gym attendance answers and reports total workout days and the longest consecutive streak. Numbered callouts (1-4) label the Prompt, Input, Process (looped), and Output stages in each transcript.
labels: For each day of the week, indicate if you worked out at the gym
You worked out 5 days with a max streak of 3 days in a row

title: CS102_Unit2a_Control_Structures
summary: Reintroduces control structures as language constructs for decision-making, listing if, switch, while, and for as the common ones relevant to this unit's focus on loops.
main_text:
We need ways of making decisions in our program:
- To repeat code until we want it to stop
- To only execute certain code if a condition is true
- To execute one segment of code or another

Language constructs that allow us to make decisions are referred to as control structures. The common ones are:
- if statements
- switch statements
- while loops
- for loops
notes_text: This is a recap of the control-structures concept previously introduced with conditionals, now setting up loops (while, for) as the focus of this unit.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Loops
summary: Introduces loops as repeatable code structures, giving real-world examples, and notes the need for a stopping condition to avoid infinite loops, previewing the three loop kinds: while, do..while, and for.
main_text:
Loops are structures of code that may be repeated some number of times.

Examples:
- Sum each student's grades (for all students in the class)
- Search through a sequence of numbers for a particular value
- Attend lecture

We need some condition to tell us when to stop looping, otherwise we'll repeat our code forever and never stop (a.k.a. an infinite loop). Several kinds of loops: 'while', 'do..while', and 'for'.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Motivation_for_Loops
summary: Section divider slide introducing the motivating rationale for why loops are needed in programming.
main_text: MOTIVATION FOR LOOPS
notes_text: This is a section-header slide marking the transition into concrete motivating examples (repetitive cout statements, guessing game) for why loops matter.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Motivation_for_Loops
summary: Motivates loops by contrasting the impracticality of writing 1000 individual cout statements to print the first 1000 positive integers against the concise equivalent using a for loop.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Why_We_Need_Loops_1
summary: Sets up a guessing-game example where the program checks a single guess against a secret number and asks what should happen if the guess is wrong, motivating the need for repetition.
notes_text: This is the first step in a three-part progression (slides 8-10) building intuition for why a single if statement is insufficient and loops are needed.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Why_We_Need_Loops_2
summary: Extends the guessing-game example by nesting a second if inside the else branch to handle a second wrong guess, again asking what should happen if the guess is still wrong.
notes_text: This builds directly on slide 8, nesting a second if-else inside the first else branch to handle a second guess attempt.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Why_We_Need_Loops_3
summary: Completes the guessing-game progression by nesting a third if for a third guess, then draws the key insight that no finite number of nested if statements can handle an arbitrary number of guesses, motivating the switch to a loop.
notes_text: This slide delivers the key pedagogical payoff of the 3-slide sequence: nested if statements cannot scale to an unbounded number of attempts, so a loop is the necessary generalization.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Types_of_Loops
summary: Introduces the two (really two-and-a-half) main kinds of loops -- while and for -- previewing their four essential parts (initialization, condition, body, update) with a side-by-side while/for code comparison.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Loop_Flowchart_4_Necessary_Parts
summary: Explains the four necessary parts of any loop (initialization, condition, body, update) and their roles, illustrated with a flowchart and matching for/while code examples counting to 1000.

images.description: A flowchart showing the four necessary parts of a loop as connected boxes: an Initialization box (e.g. i=1) feeds into a Condition diamond (e.g. i <= 1000); if true, flow proceeds to a Body box (e.g. cout << i << endl) then to an Update box (e.g. i += 1) which loops back to the Condition; if false, flow exits to 'Code after the loop'.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Type_1_while_Loops
summary: Introduces while loops as essentially a repeating if statement, comparing the flowchart and code of a single if statement to that of a while loop, highlighting the loop-back arrow as the key structural difference.
notes_text: The side-by-side flowcharts visually emphasize the loop-back arrow present in the while flowchart but absent in the if flowchart, which is the defining structural difference between the two.

images.description: Two side-by-side flowcharts contrasting an if statement and a while loop: the if flowchart shows Initialization -> Condition -> (True: If Block Statements, False: skip) -> Following statements with no loop-back; the while flowchart shows the identical structure except the while Block Statements/Update Statement box loops back up to the Condition diamond, annotated 'This is the major change between if and while'.
labels: This is the major change between if and while

title: CS102_Unit2a_Type_1_while_Loops_Trace
summary: Continues the while-loop explanation with a numbered execution trace (1 through 9, with repeated True/True/False condition checks) mapped onto the loop flowchart to show the repeated flow of control.
notes_text: This slide builds directly on the prior while-loop flowchart, adding numbered execution-order annotations to make the repeated control-flow path concrete for students learning to trace loop execution.

images.description: The same while-loop flowchart as the previous slide (Initialization -> Condition -> Body/Update -> loop back to Condition -> Code after the loop), now annotated with numbered steps 1 through 9 and True/True/False labels tracing the order in which the loop's condition, body, and update are executed across multiple iterations.

title: CS102_Unit2a_What_Goes_In_a_Loop_Body
summary: Demonstrates that any valid C++ code (expressions, assignments, function calls, if..else, even other loops) can go inside a while or for loop body, using a guessing-game example that repeatedly prompts until the correct guess is entered.
notes_text: This resolves the guessing-game motivation from slides 8-10: the while loop naturally handles an arbitrary number of guesses without needing nested if statements.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Hand_Tracing_1
summary: A hand-tracing exercise asking students to trace a while loop that repeatedly decrements a variable y by different amounts depending on its current value, for two different starting inputs (y=18 and y=6).
notes_text: This is a practice exercise; the worked solution appears later in the deck under 'Solutions While Tracing (1)'.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Hand_Tracing_2
summary: A hand-tracing exercise asking students to trace a while loop that repeatedly halves an integer x as long as it is even, for two different starting inputs (x=24 and x=27).
notes_text: This is a practice exercise; the worked solution appears later in the deck under 'Solutions While Tracing (2)'.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Type_2_for_Loops
summary: Introduces for loops as making the four parts of a while loop (initialization, condition, body, update) explicit in their syntax, comparing while and for flowcharts and syntax side by side with a counting example.

images.description: Two side-by-side flowcharts comparing a while loop and a for loop, both showing Initialization -> Condition -> Body -> Update -> loop back to Condition -> Following statements, illustrating that the for loop's flow is structurally identical to the while loop's but with initialization and update made explicit parts of the for statement's syntax.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Type_2_for_Loop_Sequencing
summary: Details the precise execution order of a for loop's parts: initialization runs once, the condition is checked before each iteration, and the update runs after each execution of the body, illustrated with a numbered trace.
notes_text: This slide is the for-loop analog of the earlier numbered while-loop trace, emphasizing that init executes exactly once while condition/body/update repeat.

images.description: A flowchart of a for loop's execution order (init runs once, then Condition -> True: For Block Statements -> Update -> back to Condition, or False: exit to Following statements) annotated with numbered steps 1 through 9 tracing the precise sequence in which init, condition, body, and update execute across several iterations.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Some_Examples_of_for
summary: Presents two worked for-loop examples with their program outputs: one counting up from 0 to 4, and another counting down by successive halving from 8 to 1, noting that the initial value, condition, and update can be any valid expression.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Tangent_Scope
summary: Introduces the concept of variable scope (lifetime and visibility) as relevant background for understanding for loops, explaining that in C/C++ a variable's scope is the curly braces it is declared within and it dies at the end of that block.
notes_text: The example demonstrates that 'temp' declared inside the if block's braces dies at the closing brace, so referencing it afterward ('temp = i++;') fails to compile; similarly, 'i' declared in main() is not visible inside the separate function f1().

title: CS102_Unit2a_Declaring_the_Inductive_Variable
summary: Explains that a for loop's initialization statement can declare a control (inductive) variable whose scope is considered to be the for loop itself, meaning it dies at the loop's end but can be reused in a subsequent loop.

title: CS102_Unit2a_A_Last_Note_on_Variables_Scope
summary: Introduces global vs. local variable scope, defining global variables as declared outside any function (visible everywhere, but disallowed in this course) and local variables as declared inside a function (visible only there), illustrated with an example.
notes_text: Important course policy note: global variables are explicitly disallowed in CS102, even though the language permits them.

title: CS102_Unit2a_for_Hand_Tracing_1
summary: A hand-tracing exercise with two for-loop programs, asking students to trace all changes to x, y, and i: one loop increments i by y while incrementing y each iteration (input '10 2'), the other increments x while decrementing y (input '4 11').
notes_text: This is a practice exercise; the worked solutions appear later in the deck under 'for Solutions 1'.

title: CS102_Unit2a_for_Hand_Tracing_2
summary: A hand-tracing exercise with two for-loop programs, asking students to trace and predict cout output: one loop counts symmetrically from -n to n (input n=-2), the other computes sine values over an angle range using a floating-point step.
notes_text: This is a practice exercise; the worked solutions appear later in the deck under 'for Solutions 2'.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Self_Study_Do_While
summary: Section divider slide introducing do..while loops as a self-study topic.
main_text: SELF STUDY: DO...WHILE
notes_text: This is a section-header slide marking do..while loops as designated self-study material.

title: CS102_Unit2a_do_while_Loops_1
summary: Introduces do..while loops as a sibling of while loops that start with the 'do' keyword, followed by a body in braces, and end with a 'while (condition);' clause, noting that the body always executes at least once.

title: CS102_Unit2a_do_while_Loops_2
summary: Compares the flowcharts of while and do..while loops, showing that do..while checks its condition after executing the body at least once, whereas while checks the condition before executing the body at all.
notes_text: The two flowcharts are structurally similar (both loop back on True), but the do..while flowchart places the condition check after the body box, visually reinforcing that the body always runs at least once before any check occurs.

images.description: Two side-by-side flowcharts comparing a while loop (Condition checked first, then True leads to while Block Statements which loops back to Condition) and a do..while loop (while Block Statements executes first, then Condition is checked, looping back to the block if True), both ending at Following statements when the condition is False, illustrating that do..while guarantees at least one execution of the body before the condition is ever checked.

title: CS102_Unit2a_do_while_Loops_3
summary: Adds a numbered execution trace (steps 1-7, True/True/False) to the do..while flowchart, reinforcing that the body executes before the condition is checked, unlike a while loop.
notes_text: This is the do..while analog of the earlier numbered while-loop and for-loop traces, showing the execution order specific to do..while's check-after-body structure.

images.description: The do..while flowchart from the previous slide, now annotated with numbered steps 1 through 7 and True/True/False labels tracing the execution order: the loop body runs first, then the condition is evaluated, looping back to the body if true or exiting to Following statements if false.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Solutions_While_Tracing_1
summary: Provides the worked solution to the earlier Hand Tracing (1) exercise, showing the traced sequence of values printed by the nested-if while loop for inputs y=18 (yielding 18, 13, 8, 5, 2, 1, 0) and y=6 (yielding 6, 3, 2, 1, 0).
notes_text: This is the answer key to the exercise on the 'Hand Tracing (1)' slide.

title: CS102_Unit2a_Solutions_While_Tracing_2
summary: Provides the worked solution to the earlier Hand Tracing (2) exercise, showing the traced sequence of values for the halving-while-even loop for inputs x=24 (yielding 24, 12, 6, 3) and x=27 (yielding just 27, since it's already odd).
notes_text: This is the answer key to the exercise on the 'Hand Tracing (2)' slide. Note the input of 27 highlights that the loop body never executes at all if the initial condition is already false, since 27 is odd.

title: CS102_Unit2a_for_Solutions_1
summary: Provides the worked solutions to the earlier 'for' Hand Tracing (1) exercise, showing the outputs for both for-loop programs: input '4 11' produces four lines pairing x and y, and input '10 2' produces the sequence 1, 4, 8.
notes_text: This is the answer key to the exercise on the 'for Hand Tracing (1)' slide.

title: CS102_Unit2a_for_Solutions_2
summary: Provides the worked solutions to the earlier 'for' Hand Tracing (2) exercise, showing that input n=2 produces the symmetric sequence -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, and inputs pi/2 and 2*pi produce the sine sequence 0, 1, 0, -1.
notes_text: This is the answer key to the exercise on the 'for Hand Tracing (2)' slide.
